sentences.text: We argued for an hour about whether the coroner or the sister should question the suicide note's authenticity first. Will the continuity bible cover the forged document's paper stock, or do I improvise as usual? By Friday I owe her forty pages, the ferry chapter, and a decision about the widow's alibi. Yesterday's call ran long; she wants the document examiner introduced two chapters earlier. Lose the forged suicide letter and book seven collapses into a routine inheritance squabble — she knows it, I know it. Voice-matching gets easier after midnight, when her clipped, present-tense rhythm starts to feel like my own pulse. Her editor flagged the handwriting-analysis scene as too technical for the series' airport-paperback readership. Does the suicide letter read as genuine on first pass, she asked, or do we tip the forgery early? Nobody outside the contract knows the suicide letter's misquoted poem was my idea, not hers. My predecessor quit over the pacing notes; I keep mine in a folder labeled "character building." Deadline math: three chapters a week until the manuscript hits her agent's desk on the first. The client called at seven to ask whether the forged suicide note should surface in chapter three or wait for the inquest scene. Three installments in, and I still ghostwrite under an NDA thicker than the manuscripts themselves. In the series bible, the detective's late wife left no note — a silence book seven finally weaponizes. She questioned whether a forged suicide letter was too dark for the series until marketing called it the strongest hook yet. Send the ferry chapter tonight, she texted, and flag every line where the detective sounds too warm. Readers of the series expect a twist by page ninety, so the suicide note must look airtight until then. Am I imitating her voice, or has she started imitating mine after six books together? Our style sheet bans semicolons in dialogue — a rule I break exactly once per installment, as a private signature. Chapter deliveries slip every time she rewrites my cliffhangers over the weekend. Sunday afternoons are the longest, because that was our drive time, the two of us and no particular destination. Thirty-one years of joint tax returns, and this spring I filed alone at a kitchen table that felt enormous. I want to write a suicide letter.
